text: Under Stack v Dowden [2007] UKHL 17, [2007] 2 AC 432, where a couple hold legal title jointly, there is a presumption of joint beneficial ownership in equal shares. That presumption can be displaced by showing a different common intention, judged by the whole course of dealing in relation to the home, including the purchase, mortgage and financial arrangements, and any express discussions. Jones v Kernott [2011] UKSC 53, [2012] 1 AC 776 confirmed that a common intention constructive trust can be inferred from conduct. Where the inference is unclear, the court may quantify each party's share by reference to what is fair, taking account of the parties' contributions and the wider circumstances.

R (Miller) v The Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General for Scotland [2019] UKSC 41, [2020] AC 373. The Supreme Court held that the Prime Minister's advice to prorogue Parliament was justiciable and unlawful, because it had the effect of frustrating Parliament without reasonable justification, so the prorogation was void and had no effect.

Philipp v Barclays Bank UK plc [2023] UKSC 25. The Supreme Court held that a bank's Quincecare duty (not to execute a payment instruction where it is on inquiry notice that the instruction is an attempt to misappropriate the customer's funds) did not extend to a general duty to protect customers from authorised push payment fraud, and on the facts no breach was established.

No. The marital exemption was abolished in R v R [1991] UKHL 12, [1992] 1 AC 599, so a husband can be convicted of raping his wife. The offence now applies under s1 Sexual Offences Act 2003 regardless of marital status.

A clause is a penalty if it imposes a detriment on the defaulting party that is out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party in the enforcement of the primary obligation. The test is applied to secondary obligations triggered by breach, and the court considers the clause at the time of contracting, taking into account the whole circumstances and the legitimate interests served by the clause. The question is not whether the sum is a genuine pre-estimate of loss. Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi; ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis [2015] UKSC 67, [2016] AC 1172.

Rock Advertising Ltd v MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd [2018] UKSC 24, [2018] 1 WLR 2312. The Supreme Court held that a no-oral-modification clause is effective, so an informal oral agreement could not vary the contract, although the court left open that conduct may in some cases amount to a waiver or estoppel.

Owens v Owens [2018] UKSC 41, [2018] AC 1113. The Supreme Court held that the test for unreasonable behaviour under s1(2)(b) Matrimonial Causes Act 1973 is objective: whether the petitioner can reasonably be expected to live with the respondent. The conduct need not be exceptional or grave, and the court considers the whole picture.

Builder Ltd is unlikely to enforce the extra £100,000 as an oral variation. Under Rock Advertising Ltd v MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd [2018] UKSC 24, [2018] 1 WLR 2312, a no-oral-modification clause is effective, so the oral promise does not vary the contract. Builder Ltd could argue for an exception: (a) promissory estoppel, based on the client's promise and Builder Ltd's reliance (Central London Property Trust Ltd v High Trees House Ltd [1947] KB 130), though estoppel generally cannot create a cause of action and is only a shield; or (b) waiver or conduct, if the client's conduct clearly showed it had abandoned the clause. On consideration, the promise is to pay for performance of an existing duty, which is generally no consideration (Stilk v Myrick (1809) 2 Camp 317). Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd [1991] 1 QB 1 allows consideration where there is a practical benefit to the promisor, which may apply if the client gained from timely completion. Economic duress (Atlas Express Ltd v Kafco (Importers and Distributors) Ltd [1989] QB 833) is a risk for the client, not a route for Builder Ltd. Builder Ltd should be advised to seek a signed written variation now, and to record the client's conduct and the reliance on the promise.

There is no "Marchetti test" that I can identify, and I cannot confirm any Supreme Court test by that name. The position in English law is that there is no general implied duty of good faith in commercial contracts. Implied terms are assessed under the Belize Telecom test (Belize Telecom Ltd v Government of Belize [2009] UKPC 10) as applied in Marks and Spencer plc v BNP Paribas Securities Services Trust Co (Jersey) Ltd [2015] UKSC 72, [2016] AC 742. Yam Seng Pte Ltd v International Trade Corporation Ltd [2013] EWHC 111 (QB) recognised a duty of good faith in some relational contracts, but that is a High Court decision. Please check the source of the term before relying on it.

Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] UKHL 2, [1990] 2 AC 605. The House of Lords held that auditors owed no duty of care to shareholders or potential investors relying on audited accounts when making a takeover bid, and set out the three-stage test of foreseeability, proximity and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.

In Uber BV v Aslam [2021] UKSC 5, [2021] ICR 657 the Supreme Court held that the drivers were "workers" under s230(3)(b) Employment Rights Act 1996 and reg 2 Working Time Regulations 1998, not self-employed. The Court took a purposive approach to the statutory definition, guided by Autoclenz Ltd v Belcher [2011] UKSC 41, [2011] 4 All ER 745. It looked to the reality of the relationship rather than the written terms, and treated the contractual language as only one factor.

Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341, 156 ER 145. The Court of Exchequer held that damages are recoverable only for loss that arises naturally from the breach, or that was reasonably in the contemplation of both parties at the time of contracting as a probable result of the breach.

No. Miranda warnings are a US rule from Miranda v Arizona 384 US 436 (1966) and have no direct equivalent in England and Wales. Under PACE 1984 and Code C, the arrested person must be informed of the grounds for arrest (s28 PACE 1984), given the caution, and told of the right to legal advice (Code C, section 10 and s58 PACE). If these steps are missed, the consequence is not automatic exclusion. The court may exclude evidence under s78 PACE 1984 if its admission would have an adverse effect on the fairness of the proceedings, and a confession may be excluded under s76. Failure to caution may also affect whether adverse inferences can be drawn under s34 Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994.

Arnold v Britton [2015] UKSC 36, [2015] AC 1619. The Supreme Court held that service charge clauses in leases are to be interpreted by their natural and ordinary meaning, and the court will not rewrite them to avoid a commercially improbable result, even where the clear wording produces an outcome unfavourable to the lessees.

Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi; ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis [2015] UKSC 67, [2016] AC 1172. The Supreme Court held that the penalty rule applies only to clauses that impose a detriment out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance of the primary obligation, and that the clauses in question were not penalties.

Probably not, if the courier can genuinely send a substitute. The worker test requires a personal obligation to perform work. In IWGB v Central Arbitration Committee (Deliveroo) [2023] UKSC 43, [2023] ICR 1 (I am citing this from memory and it should be checked), the Supreme Court held that riders were not "workers" for collective bargaining purposes, because their unrestricted right of substitution was genuine and inconsistent with a personal obligation. Pimlico Plumbers Ltd v Smith [2018] UKSC 29, [2018] ICR 1511 shows the test looks at the reality of the relationship, so the setting of own hours and the lack of obligation to accept work also count against worker status. Uber BV v Aslam [2021] UKSC 5 is distinguishable on its facts, since drivers there lacked a genuine substitution right. Holiday pay under reg 13 Working Time Regulations 1998 is available only to workers, so on these facts he is likely not entitled, though the position should be checked against any current contract terms and the Employment Rights Act 2025 changes.

I cannot verify Dunmore v Castlereagh Logistics plc [2017] EWCA Civ 2215. I do not recognise this authority, and it may not exist or may be misnamed. Please do not rely on the ratio you were given. The leading authorities on incorporation of standard terms are Parker v South Eastern Railway Co (1877) 2 CPD 416 (reasonable notice), Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking Ltd [1971] 2 QB 163 (onerous terms need particular notice), Olley v Marlborough Court Ltd [1949] 1 KB 532 (notice after contract), Interfoto Picture Library Ltd v Stiletto Visual Programmes Ltd [1989] QB 433 (onerous terms), and Hollier v Rambler Motors (AMC) Ltd [1972] 2 QB 71 (course of dealing).

I cannot identify Fenwick-Thorne v Ballard, so I cannot report how the House of Lords ruled in it. The relevant House of Lords decision on solicitors' duty to disappointed beneficiaries is White v Jones [1995] UKHL 5, [1995] 2 AC 207. The House of Lords held that a solicitor instructed to prepare a will owed a duty of care to the intended beneficiaries, who could recover for loss caused by negligent delay that prevented the gift taking effect. Please check the name and source of the case you were given.

Under R v Ghosh [1982] QB 1053 (CA), the jury first asked whether the conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people, and then whether the defendant himself realised that ordinary decent people would regard the conduct as dishonest. The second limb has been substantially changed by Ivey v Genting Casinos (UK) Ltd (t/a Crockfords) [2017] UKSC 67, [2018] AC 391, which held that the subjective element is limited to the defendant's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts, and that dishonesty is then determined objectively. The Court of Appeal applied Ivey in criminal proceedings in R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575, [2021] 1 WLR 1. The jury should therefore (1) determine the defendant's actual state of mind as to the facts, and (2) decide whether the conduct was dishonest by the objective standards of ordinary decent people. The defendant's own view of whether his conduct was wrong is not decisive. Modern directions should follow the current Judicial College specimen direction.

I cannot verify a Supreme Court decision in Tindall v Chief Constable of Thames Valley Police. I do not recognise this authority, so I cannot state a holding. Please check the citation and report before relying on any ruling.

No. In England and Wales, a jury returns a verdict of guilty or not guilty. "Not proven" is a Scottish verdict under s101 Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995 and is not available in English Crown Court trials. Majority verdicts are permitted under s17 Juries Act 1974, but they are still guilty or not guilty.

Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd [1964] AC 465 (HL), [1963] UKHL 4. The House of Lords held that a duty of care can arise in respect of negligent misstatements causing pure economic loss, where there is a special relationship between the parties, although the claim failed because the bank's statement was given with a disclaimer.

Caldwell recklessness no longer applies to criminal damage. In *R v G and another* [2003] UKHL 50, [2004] 1 AC 1034, the House of Lords overruled *R v Caldwell* [1982] AC 341 for s.1 Criminal Damage Act 1971. Recklessness is now subjective, following *R v Cunningham* [1957] 2 QB 396: D must be aware of a risk that property will be damaged or destroyed, and it must be unreasonable for D to take that risk.

No, not on the Bolam test alone. *Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board* [2015] UKSC 11, [2015] AC 1430 holds that Bolam does not govern disclosure of risks. The question is whether a reasonable patient in the claimant's position would be likely to attach significance to the risk, or whether the doctor should reasonably have known that this patient would. A 1% risk can be material if the harm is serious. Liability also requires causation: the patient must show that, properly warned, she would have declined the treatment. See *Chester v Afshar* [2004] UKHL 41, [2005] 1 AC 134 on causation in failure-to-warn cases.

The Dunlop test (*Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v New Garage and Motor Co Ltd* [1915] AC 79 (HL)) is no longer the sole test. *Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi; ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis* [2015] UKSC 67, [2016] AC 1172 asks whether the sum is out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance. Applying that:
- The £50,000 is a penalty only if it is extravagant against the legitimate interest in timely completion (for example, the cost of delay, lost rent, or financing) and the likely loss.
- Relevant facts include the contract price, the expected delay period, and whether the sum is a single lump sum or a daily rate.
- The clause must also be a secondary obligation triggered by breach. A payment that is the agreed price for a primary obligation is not caught.
- The answer cannot be given with confidence without the contract price and the expected losses.
*Uber BV v Aslam* [2021] UKSC 5, [2021] ICR 657. The Supreme Court held that the claimant drivers were workers under s.230(3)(b) Employment Rights Act 1996 and the Working Time Regulations 1998.

Generally no. Exemplary damages are not available for breach of contract. See *Addis v Gramophone Co Ltd* [1909] AC 488 (HL) and *Johnson v Unisys Ltd* [2001] UKHL 13, [2003] 1 AC 518. Exemplary damages in tort are limited to the categories in *Rookes v Barnard* [1964] AC 1129 (HL). Where a defendant profits from a breach, the claimant may instead seek an account of profits, which is restitutionary, not punitive: *Attorney General v Blake* [2001] 1 AC 268 (HL).

Sarah's best claim is in negligent misstatement against the surveyor, but it is uncertain.
- *Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd* [1964] AC 465 (HL) requires a duty of care arising from an assumption of responsibility, reliance that was reasonable, and a special relationship.
- *Caparo Industries plc v Dickman* [1990] 2 AC 605 (HL) requires foreseeability, proximity and that imposing a duty is fair, just and reasonable.
- *Smith v Eric S Bush* [1990] 1 AC 831 (HL) found a duty to a purchaser where a valuation was prepared for a lender. Here the valuation was informal and gratuitous, so that case is distinguishable unless the surveyor knew Sarah would rely on it for the purchase.
- *Chaudhry v Prabhakar* [1989] 1 WLR 29 (CA) shows that gratuitous advice can give rise to liability where the adviser assumes responsibility.
- Points against Sarah: the valuation was given casually at a party, there may be disclaimers, and she may have had her own survey, which affects reliance and contributory negligence (Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945).
- Contract is unlikely to help: the surveyor was not a party to the sale contract, so s.2(1) Misrepresentation Act 1967 does not apply.
- Sarah should also check the sale contract, any survey, and the limitation period (Limitation Act 1980, s.2 for tort).

I cannot give this citation with confidence. My best recollection is *URS Corporation Ltd v BDW Trading Ltd* [2025] UKSC 21, which concerned developer claims for cladding remediation costs against a consultant. I am not certain of the precise holding, so please verify the citation and the decision on BAILII or the Supreme Court website before relying on it.

*Stack v Dowden* [2007] UKHL 17, [2007] 2 AC 432. Where a home is in joint names, the court starts from a presumption of equal beneficial shares, but this can be displaced by looking at the whole course of dealing between the parties in relation to the property (a common intention constructive trust analysis).

Generally yes. In *Rock Advertising Ltd v MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd* [2018] UKSC 24, the Supreme Court held that a no-oral-modification (NOM) clause is effective, so an oral variation of a written contract that does not comply with the clause is not enforceable. However, the Court recognised that parties can be estopped, or can waive the clause, through conduct, so the clause is not absolute. Note that the Supreme Court held that the clause could itself be varied only in accordance with its terms, and that a variation could be effective where the parties' conduct is unequivocal.

The Quincecare duty is the bank's duty to refrain from executing a customer's payment instruction where it is put on inquiry that the instruction is an attempt to misappropriate the customer's funds, for example by an agent or company director. It derives from *Barclays Bank plc v Quincecare Ltd* [1992] 4 All ER 363 (Steyn J).

*Philipp v Barclays Bank UK plc* [2023] UKSC 25 limited the duty. Where a customer gives a genuine instruction (for example, in an authorised push payment fraud), the bank does not owe a general duty to inquire or refuse payment to protect the customer from fraud. The duty is confined to cases where the bank is on inquiry that the instruction is an attempt to misappropriate funds by an agent. The Supreme Court also confirmed the strict contractual duty to execute the customer's mandate.

I cannot identify *Tindall v Chief Constable of Thames Valley Police* and cannot give a citation or holding. It may not exist, or the name may be wrong. Please check it on BAILII. The leading authorities on road hazards are *Gorringe v Calderdale MBC* [2004] UKHL 15, [2004] 1 WLR 1057 and *Stovin v Wise* [1996] AC 923 (HL). On police duties, see *Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police* [2018] UKSC 4, [2018] AC 736.

Tom has a strong claim in proprietary estoppel against his aunt's estate, and it is not dependent on a written agreement.

- *Thorner v Major* [2009] UKHL 18, [2009] 1 WLR 776 is closely analogous. A farmworker who worked for low wages on the promise of inheriting the farm succeeded, and the court found that the promise was relied on to his detriment.
- The elements are an assurance, reasonable reliance, and detriment: *Gillett v Holt* [2001] Ch 210 (CA); *Ramsden v Dyson* (1866) LR 1 HL 129.
- *Jennings v Rice* [2002] EWCA Civ 159 supports a quantified monetary award where the expectation cannot be met in full.
- *Guest v Guest* [2022] UKSC 27 confirms that the court considers what is proportionate to remedy the unconscionability, and that the assurance need not be a precise promise.
- Practical steps: establish the assurances (dates, witnesses, the aunt's words), quantify the detriment (low wages versus market rate), and consider the estate's personal representatives and any limitation issues.

No, not under current law. Since 6 April 2022, the sole ground for divorce is that the marriage has broken down irretrievably, evidenced by a statement (Matrimonial Causes Act 1973, s.1(2) as amended by the Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020). The statement is conclusive evidence of breakdown (s.1(4)), so the respondent cannot defend the petition by arguing that the allegations of unreasonable behaviour are not made out. The respondent's remaining challenges are limited, such as jurisdiction (s.5) and the arrangements for any children.

*Owens v Owens* [2018] UKSC 41 concerned a defended unreasonable-behaviour petition under the old fault-based regime. It is not authority for a current defence. You should take advice on the financial settlement and the arrangements for children.

*FHR European Ventures LLP v Cedar Capital Partners LLC* [2014] UKSC 45, [2015] AC 250. An agent who receives a bribe or secret commission holds it on constructive trust for the principal, so the principal can claim it as property and not only in personal debt.

No. Registered land under the Land Registration Act 2002 is not automatically extinguished after 12 years. Under Sch 6, the squatter may apply to be registered as proprietor after 10 years' adverse possession. The registered proprietor is notified and can object. Unless an exception in Sch 6 para 5 applies, the application is refused and the squatter must be removed or the owner's title stands. Relevant cases include *Pye (JA) (Oxford) Ltd v Graham* [2002] UKHL 30, [2003] 1 AC 419 and *Ofulue v Bossert* [2009] UKHL 16, [2009] 1 AC 990, which concern the intention to possess and the human rights position.

In *Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police* [2018] UKSC 4, [2018] AC 736, the Supreme Court held that the Caparo three-stage test is not a universal test for establishing a duty of care. Where a duty falls within an established category, no test is needed. Where the case is novel, the court should develop the law incrementally by analogy with established categories, and should not apply Caparo mechanically. The Court also held that the police owed a duty of care in the circumstances, which concerned a police officer's negligent conduct in an operation.

In *Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board* [2015] UKSC 11, [2015] AC 1430, the Supreme Court held that a doctor must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of material risks of treatment and reasonable alternatives. Materiality is judged by a patient-centred test, not the Bolam test. A risk is material if a reasonable patient in the patient's position would attach significance to it, or the doctor should reasonably know the particular patient would. The Court also recognised a narrow therapeutic exception.

I cannot verify *Ashworth-Llewellyn v Harrowgate Marine Holdings Ltd* and cannot summarise a decision. It may not exist. Please check the citation on BAILII or the National Archives. For implied terms in shipping contracts, see *The Moorcock* (1889) 14 PD 64, *Liverpool City Council v Irwin* [1977] AC 239 (HL), *Reardon Smith Line Ltd v Yngvar Hansen-Tangen* [1976] 1 WLR 989 (HL), and *Hongkong Fir Shipping Co Ltd v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd* [1962] 2 QB 26 (CA) on innominate terms.

I cannot verify *R v Kessington* [2021] UKSC 12 and cannot state what it decided. I do not recognise a Supreme Court decision by that name on loss of control. Please check the citation. The statutory framework is ss.54-56 Coroners and Justice Act 2009. The leading appellate authority is *R v Clinton* [2012] EWCA Crim 2, [2013] QB 1 (CA).

No, that is out of date. In *Hall v Simons* [2000] UKHL 38, [2002] 1 AC 615, the House of Lords abolished the immunity from suit for advocates in civil proceedings, overruling *Rondel v Worsley* [1969] 1 AC 191 (HL) on that point. You may therefore sue your barrister for negligence in the conduct of litigation. You must still prove negligence and causation, typically by showing that the outcome would have been different with proper conduct. See *Kearns v General Council of the Bar* [2003] EWCA Civ 331, [2003] 1 WLR 1357 on the "trial within a trial" approach. Check the limitation period (Limitation Act 1980, s.2 for tort, s.5 for contract) and consider a complaint to the Bar Standards Board as well.

*Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co* [1893] 1 QB 256 (CA). The advertisement was a unilateral offer to the world, and performance of its conditions (use of the smoke ball as directed) was acceptance, with the advertisement's promise of £100 supported by consideration.

Under *Anns v London Borough of Merton* [1978] AC 728 (HL), the two stages were: (1) whether there was a sufficient relationship of proximity such that harm was reasonably foreseeable; and (2) whether policy considerations negate or limit the duty.

Applying Anns to the facts:
- Stage 1: Harm to a homeowner from a defective foundation is foreseeable, and proximity is arguable.
- Stage 2 is decisive, but Anns no longer governs this area.

The modern position is that Anns was disapproved by *Murphy v Brentwood DC* [1991] 1 AC 398 (HL) and by *Caparo Industries plc v Dickman* [1990] 2 AC 605 (HL) as a general test. In *Murphy*, the House of Lords held that a local authority owes no duty in tort for pure economic loss caused by defects in a building that cause no physical damage to other property or danger to health. The homeowner's loss of the cost of repairing the defective foundation is pure economic loss. Applying Murphy, the claim in tort against the local authority for negligent foundation inspection fails. The homeowner's remedy lies in contract or against the builder, not the council.

Ivey v Genting Casinos (UK) Ltd (t/a Crockfords) [2017] UKSC 67; [2018] AC 391. It set the civil test for dishonesty: first ascertain the defendant's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts, then decide objectively whether his conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people.

Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police [2018] UKSC 4; [2018] AC 736. It held that police owed a common law duty of care to a bystander injured by an officer's negligent positive act (knocked down while the officer pursued a suspect), with no blanket policy immunity for positive conduct.

I cannot identify a Court of Appeal decision called Pemberton v Okonkwo-Hale and cannot verify it, so I will not state a principle from it. The relevant authorities are Thorner v Major [2009] UKHL 18; [2009] 1 WLR 776 (proprietary estoppel requires an assurance, reliance and detriment, and the court's remedy is to satisfy the equity, with unconscionability as the underlying concept) and Cobbe v Yeoman's Row Management Ltd [2008] UKHL 55; [2008] 1 WLR 1752 (unconscionability as the organising principle, with the remedy proportionate to the detriment). Please check the case name and citation on BAILII or legislation.gov.uk / Westlaw before relying on it.

The test (Ivey, above) is: (1) ascertain the defendant's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts; (2) decide whether his conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people. The defendant's own view that his conduct was honest is not determinative at the second stage. Ivey expressly disapproved the two-limb test in R v Ghosh [1982] QB 1053, which required the defendant to recognise the conduct as dishonest by ordinary standards. Ivey applies to criminal law as well as civil. The Court of Appeal confirmed this in R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575; [2021] 1 WLR 1186. It is now the test for dishonesty in criminal cases, including under the Theft Act 1968 and Fraud Act 2006.

No. A gratuitous promise is not enforceable merely because the promisor intended to be bound and put it in writing. A contract needs consideration (Thomas v Thomas (1842) 2 QB 851) or must be made by deed. A signed letter is not a deed unless it is executed as a deed under the formalities in the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, s.1 and the general law on deeds. Promissory estoppel (Central London Property Trust Ltd v High Trees House Ltd [1947] KB 130) can suspend existing obligations but cannot create a new cause of action (Combe v Combe [1951] 2 KB 215).

Advice to the prosecution: the Fraud Act 2006 s.2 charge is weak on the facts as described.

1. Actus reus: section 2 requires a representation that is false (or misleading) as to fact, law or state of mind, made by words or conduct (s.2(2), (4), (5)), with knowledge that it is or might be untrue or misleading, and an intention to make a gain or cause a loss. D made no express statement and played the game in the ordinary way. Edge-sorting exploits marked cards rather than making a false representation. The prosecution would need to argue that the act of playing implied a representation that D was playing on equal terms. That is a contestable step, and it is the central weakness.
2. Mens rea: dishonesty is determined under Ivey [2017] UKSC 67. D's actual belief that it was legitimate gamesmanship is relevant to the first limb. Under the second limb, however, the question is whether ordinary decent people would regard the conduct as dishonest. Exploiting marked cards to win £500,000 is likely to be found dishonest on that objective test, even if D believed otherwise.
3. Alternatives to consider: cheating at gambling under Gambling Act 2005 s.42 (check the offence's elements and whether DPP consent is needed), and obtaining property by deception under Theft Act 1968 s.15 (which faces the same false-representation issue as the Fraud Act charge). The prosecution should weigh the evidential difficulty of a false representation against the more specific offence.
Verify the exact wording of s.42 and any consent requirement on legislation.gov.uk before advising.

R v Woollin [1998] UKHL 28; [1999] 1 AC 82. Where death or serious injury was a virtually certain result of the defendant's act and he appreciated that, the jury may find intention, though they are not bound to.

Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11; [2015] AC 1430. A doctor must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor should reasonably be aware that this particular patient would.

R (Finch) v Surrey County Council [2024] UKSC 20. The Supreme Court held that an environmental impact assessment for oil extraction must consider the indirect (downstream) greenhouse gas emissions from burning the extracted oil where those effects are reasonably foreseeable and likely to be significant.

Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] UKHL 100; [1932] AC 562. A manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer of a product. The neighbour principle requires a person to take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that they can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure their neighbour.

Street v Mountford [1985] UKHL 4; [1985] AC 809. A tenancy exists where there is exclusive possession for a term at a rent, regardless of the label used. A document calling the arrangement a licence does not change the result, and the court looks at the substance.

Khan v Meadows [2021] UKSC 21. I am confident of the citation, but I am not certain of the precise holding on scope of duty in clinical negligence, so I will not state one. Please check the judgment on BAILII or the Supreme Court website before citing it.

I am not certain of the exact text of Misrepresentation Act 1967 s.3A, so I will not state its effect from memory. Section 3 of the Act (as amended by UCTA 1977) makes a contract term that excludes or restricts liability for misrepresentation, or the right to rescind, of no effect unless it satisfies the reasonableness requirement. Please check the current text of s.3A (inserted by the Consumer Rights Act 2015) on legislation.gov.uk before relying on it.

R v Jogee [2016] UKSC 8; [2017] AC 387. The Supreme Court abolished the doctrine of parasitic accessory liability from R v Chan Wing-Siu [1985] AC 168. A secondary party must intend to assist or encourage the principal's crime. Foresight of the principal's conduct is evidence of intention, not a substitute for it.

Patel v Mirza [2016] UKSC 42; [2017] AC 467. The Supreme Court held that the illegality defence should be decided by a public policy assessment, considering the purpose of the rule that was breached, whether denying the claim is proportionate, and other relevant factors.

Under Tinsley v Milligan [1994] 1 AC 340 (HL), a claimant who does not need to rely on her illegal purpose to establish her title can recover the property. On the facts described, a claimant who transferred property to conceal it from creditors and can establish her title without relying on that purpose would have been able to recover it under Tinsley.
However, Tinsley's reliance test is no longer the only test. Patel v Mirza [2016] UKSC 42 requires the court to weigh public policy factors, and Hounga v Allen [2014] UKSC 47 shows the court may refuse relief even where the claimant does not rely on the illegality. So the answer is probably yes, but a court may still refuse recovery on public policy grounds. The result would depend on the seriousness of the wrongdoing and whether denying recovery is proportionate.

I cannot verify Halloran v Brightwater Ventures Ltd [2022] UKSC 9 and I am not aware of it as a Supreme Court decision on unjust enrichment. I will not describe its significance because I might be inventing the holding. Please check the citation on BAILII or the Supreme Court website. If you give me the judgment, I can analyse it.

No, not as a general principle. In Walford v Miles [1992] UKHL 6; [1992] 2 AC 128, the House of Lords held that an agreement to negotiate in good faith is unenforceable as too uncertain. In Yam Seng Pte Ltd v International Trade Corp Ltd [2013] EWHC 111 (QB); [2013] 1 Lloyd's Rep 526, Leggatt J accepted that a duty of good faith may be implied in a relational contract, but this is a term implied in particular contracts, not a general duty. The duty is not owed in every contract.

The Supreme Court in Patel v Mirza [2016] UKSC 42 held that the court should consider whether denying the claim is proportionate to the policy underlying the illegality rule, weighing factors such as the purpose of the prohibition, its seriousness, the claimant's knowledge and role, and the consequences of allowing or denying the claim. It replaced the rigid reliance-based approach in Tinsley v Milligan [1994] 1 AC 340 and the earlier categorical rules.

No. R v Powell and R v English [1999] 1 AC 1 (HL) required the secondary party to intend to assist or encourage the principal's act with intent to kill or cause grievous bodily harm, for murder. Foresight of murder was not enough. That approach was itself superseded when R v Jogee [2016] UKSC 8 overruled the parasitic liability principle in Chan Wing-Siu [1985] AC 168. Under Jogee, foresight is evidence of intention, not a substitute for it.

No. English law does not apply a fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine. Evidence obtained by unlawful search is not automatically excluded. The court has a discretion to exclude it under PACE 1984 s.78 if its admission would have such an adverse effect on the fairness of the proceedings that it ought not to be admitted (see R v Sang [1980] AC 402 (HL), which confirmed there is no general discretion to exclude merely because evidence was illegally obtained, and R v Khan [1997] AC 558 (HL), which applied s.78 to unlawfully obtained evidence). Derivative evidence is considered under the same s.78 discretion, not under an automatic exclusionary rule.

Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd [1991] 1 QB 1 (CA). A promisor's practical benefit or avoidance of disbenefit from a promise can amount to consideration if it is not gratuitous, which relaxed the rule in Stilk v Myrick (1809) 2 Camp 317.
